chunk-001:c001.proposition: Because no contingent object contains the reason for its own existence, the totality of contingent objects requires a sufficient reason external to that totality.

orphanFallback.rationale: Copleston presents this directly as his affirmative inference from the aggregate of contingent objects to an external reason, so it is independently intelligible as a constructive move.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Although the existence of a contingent being must be learned from experience, once such a being is known to exist, the inference to a necessary being follows with necessity.

orphanFallback.rationale: The distinction between an empirically discovered contingent premise and the necessity of the resulting conditional supplies a standalone modal argument even without Russell's earlier restriction on necessity.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: God is inferred from experience rather than known a priori, and divine essence and existence must be identical because otherwise God's existence would require a sufficient reason beyond God.

orphanFallback.rationale: Copleston's experience-first inference and his reason for identifying divine essence with existence together form a self-contained account of the necessary terminus.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: The basic mystical awareness of a loving, transcendent, nonconceptual reality is more adequately explained by an objective cause than as an experience produced wholly within the subject.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source explicitly offers an objective cause as the most adequate positive explanation of mystical experience, without depending on any prior opposing move.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-03.proposition: Goodness is not identical with God in a pantheistic sense, but what is truly good reflects and proceeds from God, though this interpretation depends on independently recognizing God's existence.

orphanFallback.rationale: The source supplies a qualified positive account of the relation between objective goodness and God while expressly limiting its evidential reach, so the proposition can stand constructively.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-05.proposition: Differences in felt response cannot by themselves settle whether a judgment is sound, because without an objective criterion beyond feeling there is no basis for condemning even atrocious conduct.

orphanFallback.rationale: Copleston's color-perception comparison independently argues that divergent subjective responses do not exclude objective standards, a material criterion when assessing competing experiential reports.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-06.proposition: The perception of values and consciousness of moral obligation are best explained by a transcendent ground of value and a non-arbitrary author of moral law.

orphanFallback.rationale: This is Copleston's direct affirmative moral argument, expressly deriving a transcendent and non-arbitrary ground from common awareness of value, law, and obligation.

chunk-002:chunk-002-candidate-08.proposition: The possibility of criticizing culturally accepted moral codes presupposes an objective ideal moral order whose obligatory character can be recognized and whose real foundation is God.

orphanFallback.rationale: The inference from meaningful criticism of accepted codes to an objective ideal order and divine foundation is fully stated in the source and can operate as an affirmative argument.
